blocks.title: What a main idea is
blocks.body: The main idea is the point the whole passage makes. Details — examples, reasons, figures — exist to support it. A quick test: if most sentences can be read as evidence for an option, that option is the main idea.

blocks.title: See it on a short passage

passage.label: Practice passage (written by MockMob)
sentences: Many cities are planting trees along roads to fight summer heat.
Shade stops pavements and walls from absorbing as much sunlight during the day.
Leaves also release water vapour, which cools the air around them.
Residents of tree-lined streets often say their afternoons feel cooler.
Planners warn, however, that young trees need regular watering for their first few years if they are to survive.

blocks.body: Sentence 1 makes the claim; sentences 2–4 explain or illustrate it; sentence 5 adds a limit. A good main-idea option covers both the claim and the limit: street trees can cool a city, but they need care to survive.

blocks.title: Three wrong options you will meet
rows: One true detail, such as “Leaves release water vapour.”
It supports the main idea but is not the whole point
“Trees are the cheapest way to cool a city.”

blocks.context: Many cities are planting trees along roads to fight summer heat. Shade stops pavements and walls from absorbing as much sunlight during the day. Leaves also release water vapour, which cools the air around them. Residents of tree-lined streets often say their afternoons feel cooler. Planners warn, however, that young trees need regular watering for their first few years if they are to survive.
blocks.prompt: Which option best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Street trees can make cities cooler, but young trees need care to survive.
Trees are the cheapest way to cool a city.
optionNotes: True, but it is one supporting detail — too narrow.
Wider than anything the passage discusses — too broad.
The passage never says this — not stated.
blocks.explanation: It covers the claim (sentence 1), the support (2–4) and the limit (5). This is an unscored learning check.

units.title: Sacrificing and gaining ratios
units.summary: Work out who gave up profit share and who gained it, one partner at a time.
objectives: Calculate a partner’s sacrifice or gain from old and new shares
Turn individual sacrifices into a sacrificing ratio
Know when the old ratio is also the sacrificing ratio
units.examLink: CUET Accountancy questions on admission, retirement and change in ratio usually need this step before goodwill or capital adjustments.

sourceRefs.label: NCERT Accountancy Part I, ch. 2 Admission of a Partner (sections 2.3, 2.4, 2.7)
sourceRefs.permission: reference only; MockMob explanations and examples are original

sourceRefs.label: NCERT Accountancy Part I, ch. 3 Retirement/Death of a Partner (section 3.3)
sourceRefs.permission: reference only; MockMob explanations and examples are original

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.body: Whenever partners change how they share profit — a partner joins, a partner retires, or everyone simply agrees a new ratio — some shares fall and some rise. The partners whose shares fall are compensated, for example through the new partner’s premium for goodwill, so most questions on reconstitution start by asking who sacrificed and who gained.

blocks.title: Start with the change in share
blocks.body: For each partner, sacrifice = old share − new share. Gain = new share − old share. Use a common denominator before subtracting. A positive sacrifice means the share fell; a negative sacrifice means it rose.
blocks.formula: Sacrifice = Old share − New share · Gain = New share − Old share

blocks.title: The four-line method
steps: Write each partner’s old share and new share as fractions.
Put all of them over one common denominator.
Subtract old − new for every partner.
Positive results are sacrifices. Write them as a ratio in lowest terms.

blocks.title: Work one partner at a time
blocks.body: A and B used to share 3:2. C joins, and the new ratio A:B:C is 5:3:2. A: 3/5 − 5/10 = 1/10. B: 2/5 − 3/10 = 1/10. A and B sacrifice equally, so the sacrificing ratio is 1:1.

blocks.title: No new partner: someone still gains
blocks.body: X, Y and Z share 3:2:1 and decide to share equally. Over 6: X goes from 3/6 to 2/6, a sacrifice of 1/6. Y stays at 2/6, so nothing changes. Z goes from 1/6 to 2/6, a gain of 1/6. Z must compensate X.

blocks.title: The old ratio is not a universal shortcut
blocks.body: The old ratio describes the starting shares. The new ratio describes the final shares. Neither automatically describes the change. When a new ratio is given, compare the shares. Use the old ratio as the sacrificing ratio when the incoming share is taken in that ratio.
blocks.note: If a question says nothing about how the new partner takes the share, assume it comes from the old partners in their old ratio.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.prompt: A partner’s old share is 3/5 and new share is 1/2. What did the partner sacrifice?
blocks.explanation: 3/5 − 1/2 = 6/10 − 5/10 = 1/10. This is an unscored learning check.

blocks.title: Try a shortcut question
blocks.prompt: A and B share 3:2. C is admitted for 1/5 share, which C takes from A and B in their old ratio. What is the sacrificing ratio of A and B?
optionNotes: 1:1 would be right only if A and B gave up equal amounts.
4:1 is the ratio of the remaining 4/5 to C’s 1/5, not a sacrifice.
2:3 reverses the partners.
blocks.explanation: C takes the share in the old ratio, so A gives 3/5 of 1/5 = 3/25 and B gives 2/5 of 1/5 = 2/25. The sacrificing ratio is 3:2 — here the old ratio does apply.

blocks.prompt: A and B share profits 3:2. C is admitted and the new ratio A:B:C is 4:3:3. What is the sacrificing ratio of A and B?
blocks.explanation: A: 6/10 − 4/10 = 1/5. B: 4/10 − 3/10 = 1/10. So the sacrificing ratio is 2:1.
blocks.title: Now a calculated ratio

units.summary: Decide which side of the Revaluation Account each change goes to, then share the result correctly.
objectives: Place each change on the debit or credit side of the Revaluation Account
Calculate the net gain or loss

units.examLink: CUET questions often give four or five changes and ask for the gain or loss, or one partner’s share of it.

sourceRefs.label: NCERT Accountancy Part I, ch. 2 Admission of a Partner (sections 2.3, 2.4, 2.7)
sourceRefs.permission: reference only; MockMob explanations and examples are original

blocks.title: Why revalue before admitting a partner
blocks.body: Book values may no longer match current values. Before a new partner joins, assets are revalued, liabilities are reassessed, and anything unrecorded is brought into the books. The result belongs to the partners who ran the firm until now, so the gain or loss goes to the old partners in their old profit-sharing ratio.

blocks.title: Which side does each change go to?
blocks.note: Ask one question: does this change make the firm better off (credit) or worse off (debit)?

blocks.title: A complete example
blocks.body: A and B share 3:2 and admit C. Machinery increased: ₹10,000. Stock decreased: ₹4,000. Unrecorded liability found: ₹2,000. Creditors reduced: ₹1,000. Gains total ₹11,000; losses total ₹6,000. Net gain ₹5,000, shared 3:2: A gets ₹3,000, B gets ₹2,000. C gets nothing from it.
rows: Net gain, transferred to A and B in 3:2

blocks.title: The journal entries in one line each
steps: Increase in an asset: Asset A/c Dr. To Revaluation A/c.
Decrease in an asset: Revaluation A/c Dr. To Asset A/c.
Increase in a liability: Revaluation A/c Dr. To Liability A/c.
Decrease in a liability: Liability A/c Dr. To Revaluation A/c.
Gain transferred: Revaluation A/c Dr. To old partners’ capital accounts (old ratio).
Loss transferred: Old partners’ capital accounts Dr. (old ratio) To Revaluation A/c.

blocks.title: The two most common slips
blocks.body: Sharing the revaluation result with the new partner, or sharing it in the new ratio. Both are wrong: the new partner was not there while those values changed.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.prompt: A building is revalued upward by ₹20,000 on admission. Which entry records it?
options: Building A/c Dr. To Revaluation A/c
Revaluation A/c Dr. To Building A/c
Building A/c Dr. To Partners’ Capital A/cs
Revaluation A/c Dr. To Partners’ Capital A/cs
optionNotes: That records a decrease in the building’s value.
The gain passes through the Revaluation Account first.
That entry transfers a final gain, not one asset change.
blocks.explanation: An increase in an asset is a gain: debit the asset, credit Revaluation A/c. This is an unscored learning check.

blocks.title: Share the result
blocks.prompt: Revaluation shows gains of ₹12,000 and losses of ₹7,000. A and B share 3:2 and admit C. How much is credited to A (in ₹)?

units.subject: business_studies
units.title: Delegation and decentralisation
units.summary: Tell a manager sharing work apart from a company spreading decision-making to every level.
objectives: Name the three elements of delegation and which way each flows
Know what can and cannot be delegated
Classify a scenario as delegation or decentralisation
units.examLink: CUET Business Studies often describes a workplace situation and asks which concept, element or basis of difference it shows.

sourceRefs.label: NCERT Business Studies Part I, ch. 5 Organising
sourceRefs.permission: reference only; MockMob explanations and scenarios are original

blocks.title: Delegation: sharing work, keeping answerability
blocks.body: A manager cannot do every task personally, so authority is passed down to a subordinate to act on the manager’s behalf. The subordinate accepts the duty to do the job well. But the manager is still answerable to their own superior for the final outcome.
blocks.note: Authority is delegated, responsibility is assumed, accountability is imposed.

blocks.title: The three elements
rows: Obligation to do the assigned task
blocks.note: Authority given should match the responsibility: too much authority risks misuse; too little makes the person ineffective.

blocks.title: Delegation vs decentralisation
rows: Compulsory: no one can do every task alone
Optional policy chosen by top management
Less control, more freedom for executives
The result of a top-management policy
Narrow: a superior and immediate subordinate
Wide: extends to the lowest level

blocks.title: Two situations, side by side
blocks.body: Ritu, a regional sales manager, lets Arjun approve customer discounts up to 5% this month. Ritu is still answerable to her own boss for the month’s sales. That is delegation. The board of a retail chain decides that every store manager will hire local staff and set local offers. That is decentralisation: a policy that spreads decision-making down to the lowest level.

blocks.title: The usual trap
blocks.body: Thinking that once a task is handed over, the manager is no longer answerable. Accountability cannot be delegated at all. A second trap: calling every handover “decentralisation”. Decentralisation is delegation extended systematically across levels as a policy.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.prompt: Which element cannot be delegated at all?
optionNotes: Authority is exactly what is delegated.
Responsibility cannot be entirely delegated, but it is assumed by the subordinate.
Accountability always stays with the delegating manager.
blocks.explanation: The manager remains answerable for the outcome even after delegating. This is an unscored learning check.

blocks.prompt: A company’s top management decides that branch heads in every city will approve their own budgets and purchases. Which concept does this show?
blocks.explanation: It is a policy decision by top management that extends authority across levels.
optionNotes: Delegation is one superior sharing authority with an immediate subordinate; this is a policy across levels.
blocks.title: Classify the situation

units.subject: business_studies
units.title: Planning, controlling and the control process
units.summary: See why planning and controlling depend on each other, and name each step of control in a real situation.
objectives: Explain how planning and controlling depend on each other
Order the five steps of the controlling process
Apply critical point control and management by exception
units.examLink: CUET Business Studies frequently describes a manager’s action and asks which step of controlling it is.

sourceRefs.label: NCERT Business Studies Part I, ch. 8 Controlling
sourceRefs.permission: reference only; MockMob explanations and scenarios are original

blocks.title: Planning and controlling need each other
blocks.body: Planning sets the standards; controlling checks whether performance matches them and corrects the gap. Without a plan there is nothing to control against, and a plan nobody checks is just a wish.
blocks.note: Planning without controlling is meaningless; controlling is blind without planning.

blocks.title: “Planning looks ahead, controlling looks back” — only partly true
rows: Prescriptive: decides what should be done
Ahead, but guided by past experience
Back at results, but corrective action improves the future

blocks.title: One month in a factory
blocks.body: Standard: 1,000 units a month with at most 2% defective. Measurement: 960 units, 3% defective. Comparison: output 40 units short, defects 1 point over. Analysis: a machine was down for two days and a new operator was untrained. Corrective action: repair schedule and operator training.

blocks.title: Where managers focus
blocks.body: Critical point control: watch the key result areas whose failure hurts the whole organisation, not every activity. Management by exception: only significant deviations beyond an accepted limit go to senior management; trying to control everything ends up controlling nothing.

blocks.prompt: A store manager finds sales were ₹8 lakh against a target of ₹10 lakh. Which step of controlling is this?
blocks.explanation: Actual performance is being compared with the standard.
optionNotes: “Setting performance standards” is step 1; this situation is step 3.
“Measurement of actual performance” is step 2; this situation is step 3.
“Analysing deviations” is step 4; this situation is step 3.
“Taking corrective action” is step 5; this situation is step 3.
blocks.title: Try it
Which principle?
blocks.prompt: Labour cost may rise up to 2% without a report; only bigger increases go to senior managers. Which principle is this?
optionNotes: Critical point control is about choosing the key areas to watch, not the reporting limit.
The standard already exists; this is about which deviations are reported.
This is a control principle, not an organising policy.
blocks.explanation: Only significant deviations beyond the accepted limit are brought to management. This is an unscored learning check.

units.subject: economics
units.title: What GDP counts: final goods and value added
units.summary: Count each product once: final goods only, or the value each firm adds.
objectives: Classify a good as final or intermediate from how it is used
Calculate value added and avoid double counting
Separate gross and net value added
Recognise activity that GDP leaves out
units.examLink: CUET Economics asks you to classify goods, calculate value added, and spot what national income misses.

sourceRefs.label: NCERT Introductory Macroeconomics, ch. 2 National Income Accounting
sourceRefs.permission: reference only; MockMob explanations and examples are original

blocks.title: GDP adds up final goods, measured in money
blocks.body: Final goods are not transformed any further: consumption goods for households and capital goods such as machines that firms keep using. Intermediate goods are inputs used up in making something else, such as steel sheets for cars or copper for utensils. Money is the common measuring rod, because tonnes of rice and metres of cloth cannot be added directly.

blocks.title: Why intermediate goods are left out
blocks.body: The price of a final good already includes the inputs that went into it. Counting the inputs separately as well would count them twice — the error called double counting.

blocks.title: Value added: count each firm’s own contribution
blocks.body: Add up every firm’s output and you get ₹230 — too much, because cotton and yarn are counted again inside the cloth. Count only value added (output − inputs bought): ₹40 + ₹30 + ₹50 = ₹120, exactly the value of the final cloth.

blocks.title: Gross or net: what happens to wear and tear
blocks.body: Machines wear out as they are used. This wear and tear is depreciation, also called consumption of fixed capital. Gross value added includes it; net value added subtracts it.
blocks.formula: Gross value added = Output − Intermediate goods · Net value added = Gross value added − Depreciation

blocks.title: What GDP misses
blocks.body: Activity that is not exchanged for money is not registered: domestic work done at home without pay, and barter exchanges where goods are swapped directly. GDP therefore underestimates such activity. That is one reason GDP is not a complete measure of welfare.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.prompt: Flour bought by a bakery and used up in making bread this year is…
optionNotes: The flour is transformed into bread, so it is not final.
Capital goods are kept and used over years; flour is used up.
It is produced, but its value reaches GDP through the bread.
blocks.explanation: It is used up as an input, so its value is already inside the bread. This is an unscored learning check.

blocks.prompt: A bakery produces goods worth ₹300 and uses up inputs bought from other firms worth ₹120. What is its value added (in ₹)?
blocks.explanation: Value added = value of output − intermediate goods used = ₹300 − ₹120 = ₹180.
blocks.title: Calculate value added

units.subject: economics
units.title: Nominal GDP, real GDP and the deflator
units.summary: Separate a change in production from a change in prices.
objectives: Calculate nominal and real GDP from quantities and prices
Calculate and interpret the GDP deflator
Explain why real GDP is used for comparison
units.examLink: CUET questions give two of nominal GDP, real GDP and the deflator and ask for the third, or ask what a change means.

sourceRefs.label: NCERT Introductory Macroeconomics, ch. 2 National Income Accounting
sourceRefs.permission: reference only; MockMob explanations and examples are original

blocks.title: A bigger GDP number is not always more production
blocks.body: If GDP measured at this year’s prices doubles, production might have doubled — or prices alone might have doubled while output stayed the same. To compare years, or countries, we need a measure that holds prices fixed.

blocks.title: Notebook country
blocks.body: Base year: 200 notebooks at ₹20. This year: 220 notebooks at ₹25. Nominal GDP = 220 × ₹25 = ₹5,500. Real GDP = 220 × ₹20 = ₹4,400. Deflator = 5500 ÷ 4400 × 100 = 125: prices are 1.25 times the base year.

blocks.title: Two formulas, rearranged
steps: GDP deflator = Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP × 100
Real GDP = Nominal GDP ÷ GDP deflator × 100
A deflator of 100 means current prices equal base-year prices.

blocks.title: Reading the deflator
blocks.body: A deflator of 125 does not mean production rose 25%. It means the price level is 1.25 times the base year’s. Output change is read from real GDP.

blocks.prompt: Nominal GDP is ₹6,000 crore and real GDP is ₹5,000 crore. What is the GDP deflator (as an index, base = 100)?
blocks.explanation: Deflator = nominal ÷ real × 100 = 6000 ÷ 5000 × 100 = 120.
blocks.title: Try it

blocks.prompt: Nominal GDP is ₹9,000 crore and the GDP deflator is 150. What is real GDP (in ₹ crore)?
blocks.explanation: Real GDP = nominal ÷ deflator × 100 = 9000 ÷ 150 × 100 = 6000.
blocks.title: Rearrange it

blocks.title: Apply current ratio
blocks.body:
Current assets are ₹60,000 and current liabilities are ₹30,000.

60,000 ÷ 30,000 = 2, or 2:1.
blocks.note: Current uses all current assets.

blocks.title: Apply quick assets
blocks.body:
Current assets of ₹60,000 include inventory of ₹15,000 and prepaid expenses of ₹5,000.

Quick assets = 60,000 − 15,000 − 5,000 = ₹40,000.
blocks.note: Inventory and prepayments are not quick cash.

blocks.title: Apply quick ratio
blocks.body:
Quick assets are ₹40,000 and current liabilities are ₹20,000.

40,000 ÷ 20,000 = 2, or 2:1.
blocks.note: Quick uses the narrower asset measure.

blocks.title: Avoid the usual mix-up
blocks.body: A ratio is not a guarantee of solvency. Do not leave prepaid expenses inside quick assets.
